doc.title: Ken Peplowski interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Hating labels; calling himself an interpreter
summary: Resisting the swing-revival label and his varied projects, calling himself an interpreter of songs.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: You’ve done some recording with Randy Sandke, right?
And some of the stuff I’ve heard you do with him is very Boppish.

So I wouldn’t think that you’re — I suppose some of the press you’re getting is more that you’re, as Scott says, “Ken has helped to keep the tradition of a small group swing alive” in one of the books. But that’s not all you’re doing.

That’s not all I do and I just hate labels like that. Because as somebody gives you a label, even if they’re well meaning, that’s what you become in everybody’s eyes. Or it becomes a jazz fact if it’s published in the books. I just hate those kind of things. And if you look back through a lot of interviews with older musicians — Duke always hated that too, or Sonny Stitt hated to be called a Charlie Parker imitator. And I hate to even have to justify what I do, but like the last few records, I did this thing with an orchestra, we did all this twentieth century music, modern classical music. The last one I did with a big band we did this pretty out piece, this concerto that was written for me. And I’ve played John Coltrane tunes and worked with Tom Harrell. I just consider myself a musician. And I don’t think about these labels. In fact I try really hard not to because I don’t want to paint myself in the same box as somebody else, even if they’re well meaning. Sometimes it can backfire. Especially because I play the clarinet and I like to play songs that may have been written in the first half of this century, people don’t even listen to the way you play, they just say Benny Goodman, swing. Sometimes that can work to your advantage, because you can get away with a lot on stage. You can play to an older, more conservative audience and you’re playing a Thelonious Monk tune or you throw in a © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-

Coltrane tune, and they’ve got their eyes closed and they’re thinking Benny Goodman swing. So it’s fine. It’s okay. But I think I tend to bristle any time any label comes up, even if it’s well meaning.
Yeah. It’s like you want to get the press—
But it’s always kind of like oooh — did he have to say that?
